topic: Sentence Improvement — substituting the underlined part with the best alternative
description: Sentence improvement: identify grammatically or stylistically incorrect underlined phrase, choose the best replacement — subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, idiom, word choice, redundancy.

questions.stem: He is one of those students who (works) hard every day. Choose the best improvement for the underlined word.

options.option_text: work — the antecedent of 'who' is 'students' (plural), so plural verb needed
works — treats 'one' as the antecedent, a common but grammatically debated error
has worked — unnecessary shift to present perfect without contextual support
No improvement required — the original 'works' is incorrect here

questions.explanation: RULE: 'one of those + noun + who' — the relative clause 'who' refers to the PLURAL noun ('students'), not 'one'. Therefore the verb after 'who' must be PLURAL: 'work'. CORRECT: 'He is one of those students who WORK hard.' CONTRAST: 'He is the only one of those students who WORKS hard' — here 'the only one' makes the antecedent singular. This is a classic grammar trap in IBPS, SSC, and banking English sections.

questions.stem: The committee (have decided) to postpone the meeting. Choose the best improvement for the underlined phrase.

options.option_text: has decided — collective nouns acting as a unit take singular verb in formal/Indian English
have decided — this is acceptable in British English but marked wrong in Indian exam context
had been deciding — unnecessary past perfect progressive for a simple decision
No improvement needed — exams expect singular verb for collective noun in Indian English

questions.explanation: RULE (Indian exam standard): collective nouns (committee, jury, team, class, family) acting as a SINGLE UNIT take a SINGULAR verb. 'The committee HAS decided' is the expected answer in IBPS PO, SSC, and state PSC exams. BRITISH ENGLISH NOTE: 'The committee have decided' is acceptable in BrE when members act individually, but Indian competitive exams consistently apply the singular rule. EXAM PATTERN: committee, jury, government, parliament, staff, crew — all singular in Indian English exam answers.

questions.stem: She told me that she (will finish) the report by Friday. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: would finish — reported speech shifts 'will' to 'would' (sequence of tenses)
will finish — correct in direct speech but wrong after past reporting verb 'told'
had finished — past perfect implies completion before another past event; not appropriate here
should finish — 'should' introduces obligation/recommendation, changing the meaning entirely

questions.explanation: SEQUENCE OF TENSES: when the reporting verb is past ('told'), the reported clause must also shift to a past form. 'will' → 'would'. CORRECT: 'She told me that she WOULD FINISH the report by Friday.' FULL SHIFT TABLE: am/is→was; are→were; has/have→had; will→would; can→could; may→might; shall→should. EXCEPTION: universal truths and reported questions keep present tense ('He said that the Earth is round'). PYQ: sequence-of-tenses in indirect speech is heavily tested in IBPS PO/Clerk English.

questions.stem: Neither the manager nor the employees (was) aware of the new policy. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: were — with neither…nor, verb agrees with the nearer subject ('employees', plural)
was — applies singular agreement to 'manager' (the farther subject) by mistake
are — wrong tense; past context requires past verb form here (not this)
have been — present perfect is incompatible with the past-tense context of the sentence

questions.explanation: NEITHER…NOR RULE: verb agrees with the subject CLOSEST (nearer) to the verb. Here: 'the manager' (singular) OR 'the employees' (plural) — 'employees' is nearer → WERE. CORRECT: 'Neither the manager nor the employees WERE aware.' EITHER…OR works the same way. MEMORY TRICK: 'ProxiMate rule' — agree with the proximate (nearest) subject. IBPS/SSC PATTERN: this is one of the top-tested neither/nor/either/or agreement rules.

questions.stem: The news (are) shocking to all of us. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: is — 'news' is a singular uncountable noun in English despite ending in -s
are — treats 'news' as plural due to the -s ending, which is incorrect
were — past tense inappropriate when no past context is established in the sentence
have been — present perfect progressive does not fit a state expressed by an adjective

questions.explanation: SINGULAR UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS ENDING IN -S: news, mathematics, physics, economics, athletics, billiards, measles, mumps — all take SINGULAR verbs. 'The news IS shocking.' Other examples: 'Mathematics IS difficult.' 'Physics IS my favourite subject.' PLURAL EXCEPTION: 'The goods ARE ready' (goods = countable plural). EXAM SHORTCUT: if the -s noun refers to a subject of study or a concept treated as a single entity, it's singular.

questions.stem: He is used to (work) late in the office. Choose the best improvement for the underlined word.

options.option_text: working — 'used to + VERB-ing' means accustomed to; -ing form required after preposition 'to'
work — confuses 'used to work' (past habit) with 'be used to working' (accustomed to)
have worked — present perfect after 'to' is ungrammatical in this structure
No improvement needed — 'work' after 'used to' is the past-habit form, not this structure

questions.explanation: TWO DIFFERENT STRUCTURES: (1) USED TO + bare infinitive = past habit that no longer happens. 'He used to WORK late' (he no longer does). (2) BE/GET USED TO + V-ing = accustomed to (can be present or past). 'He IS USED TO WORKING late' (he is accustomed to it now). The sentence says 'He is used to...' so structure (2) applies → gerund 'working'. EXAM TRAP: this distinction between the two 'used to' structures is tested in nearly every IBPS PO/Clerk English paper.

questions.stem: The teacher, as well as her students, (are) attending the seminar. Choose the best improvement.

options.option_text: is — 'as well as' is a parenthetical addition; the main subject 'the teacher' (singular) governs the verb
are — treats 'the teacher + students' as a compound subject joined by 'and', which is incorrect
were — tense change unjustified without past-time context in the sentence (not this)
have been — aspect change inappropriate for a simple ongoing state or action (not this)

questions.explanation: PARENTHETICAL ADDITION RULE: phrases like 'as well as', 'along with', 'together with', 'in addition to', 'besides', 'accompanied by' — when inserted between subject and verb — do NOT change the number of the verb. VERB AGREES with the MAIN (grammatical) subject alone. 'The teacher' = singular → IS. CONTRAST: 'The teacher AND her students are attending' — here 'and' creates a compound subject → plural verb. PYQ: 'as well as' agreement appears in virtually every IBPS PO/Clerk session-1 or session-2 English paper.
